title: Data: Moving Beyond the Colors
author: elana270
summary: A first-grade teacher and instructional leader describes a data analysis project her team conducted examining the gap between end-of-year kindergarten DIBELS scores and actual readiness for first-grade reading. The colors looked good: 81% at or above proficiency on Nonsense Word Fluency (letter-sound) and 87% on NWF decoding. But when the team looked past the colors to the actual reading behavior, they found that only 3-5 of those same students could blend a CVC word in one try — the rest were recoding (sounding out each sound and then blending, e.g., 'c-a-t, cat'). Students who could recode accurately enough to hit cut scores would not be prepared for the oral reading fluency passages they'd encounter in first grade. The author draws out a broader principle: data can be powerful but misleading when it is read at the color level rather than the behavior level, and the only way to bridge the gap is to understand what the data is actually measuring and adjust instruction accordingly. Practical instructional suggestions offered include continuous blending and 'fast way' reading.
points: Colors (blue/green/yellow/red) in assessment dashboards are a summary abstraction, not the data itself — a student can hit the cut score through a less efficient reading behavior (recoding) that will not transfer to connected text fluency.

The kindergarten-to-first-grade gap is structural, not just an individual readiness problem: when the EOY kindergarten assessment does not require fluent blending to achieve proficiency, the system has a design flaw that produces misleading readiness signals.

Continuous blending and 'fast way' reading (fading from sounding out to reading the whole word immediately) are minor instructional adjustments that have a major impact on whether students can transfer isolated word skills to connected text.

The purpose of data collection is to change instruction: data that is examined, understood, and then filed without changing what teachers do in the classroom has no value and may produce false confidence.

Teams must go three steps: first, awareness of the gap in the curriculum; second, understanding what the data actually shows at the behavior level; third, adjusting instruction to eliminate the gap — most teams stop after step one.
quotes: 81% of students at or above proficiency on the Nonsense Word Fluency (NWF) letter/sound measure, and 87% at or above proficiency on the NWF decoding measure. The colors look great. Mostly blue and green for above and benchmark, but when we look past the colors to the behaviors of reading, we noticed that only between three to five of those same students can blend a CVC word in one try.

The rest of the students, while pretty accurate, are saying each sound and recoding (e.g., 'c-a-t, cat'). To attain proficiency on the NWF benchmark at the end of kindergarten, a student needs to read 31 sounds and 7 words. Many of our students, even after recoding, were able to attain these cut scores.
On paper, our kindergarten students look ready, but when they get to first grade, their first decodable text is a full-page story with sentences. They are not prepared.

This is not to say that they won't learn, of course, many children will, but many children will struggle with this particular skill well into the school year, delaying their ability to read text fluently.
While colors look nice, they don't tell the whole story.
Once your team has taken the time to really understand the data, then it is time to change your instruction. Otherwise, there is little value in collecting the data.
Data can be powerful, but it can also be misleading. These are the types of tweaks that mean the difference between acceleration and stagnation.
